Traditional spoken dialogue systems struggle to feel natural because their complex pipelines of independent components, such as ASR and TTS, induce several seconds of latency between interactions [S2][S3]. These systems use text as the intermediate modality, which causes them to lose non-linguistic information like emotion, accent, and non-speech sounds [S2][S3]. Furthermore, they rely on a segmentation into speaker turns, which fails to handle overlapping speech, interruptions, and interjections that occur in natural conversations [S2][S3]. This turn-based approach is ill-suited for full-duplex communication where the boundary between speaker turns is non-existent [S1][S3]. Consequently, the resulting experience falls far short of the responsiveness and dynamic nature of human dialogue [S3].

record.text: Moshi is a multi-stream speech-to-speech Transformer designed for full-duplex real-time dialogue [S1]. It is built on Helium, a 7B parameter text LLM that provides strong reasoning abilities [S1][S2]. To encode audio into discrete units, it uses Mimi, a neural audio codec that combines semantic and acoustic information [S1][S2]. The system employs a Depth Transformer to jointly model user and Moshi audio streams along with text tokens [S1]. Inner Monologue is a method that generates text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens to exploit text modality knowledge [S1][S2]. This architecture allows the model to speak and listen simultaneously without explicitly modeling speaker turns [S1].

record.text: Inner Monologue is a method within the Moshi model that generates text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens while maintaining compatibility with streaming inference [S2]. It enables streaming Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) by delaying text tokens by 2 seconds, allowing the model to listen to audio content before generating text [S1]. This ASR setup operates by using ground truth audio tokens and discarding the model's audio predictions, effectively sampling only the text tokens [S3]. Conversely, it provides streaming Text-to-Speech (TTS) by delaying audio tokens by 2 seconds, which gives the text tokens lookahead and dictates the audio content based on the text [S1]. This TTS configuration uses teacher forcing on the text tokens during inference, where the model generates audio dictated by the preceding text sequence [S3]. The system achieves this functionality solely by adjusting the delay hyper-parameter between text and audio tokens, without altering the architecture, loss, or training data [S3].

record.text: In H-Net, the encoder network processes raw data and compresses it into fewer vectors with richer semantic embeddings [S3]. The decoder network subsequently upsampled these representations to reconstruct the sequence at its original resolution [S1][S3]. Both the encoder and decoder networks operate on the original resolution or fine-grained input bytes, unlike the main network which handles compressed chunks [S1][S3]. These components are strongly improved by using State Space Models (SSMs) due to their inductive bias for compression [S1]. SSMs are preferred over Transformers for these roles because they compress information into fixed-size states, aligning with the hierarchical architecture's chunking mechanism [S2].

record.text: H-Net decides where to cut the byte stream by learning content- and context-dependent discrete segmentation strategies through standard gradient-based optimization [S2]. In single-stage configurations, the model predominantly places boundaries at whitespace characters, mirroring the delimiters used by SpaceByte [S1]. The first stage of the hierarchical two-stage model combines these spacelike boundaries with the initial characters of each word [S1]. The process is not based on static rules, as H-Net often merges multiple words and spacelike characters based on specific content [S1]. Perturbation analysis demonstrates that boundaries are drawn based on content and context, continuing to split between semantic words even when whitespace is removed [S1]. The second stage of the hierarchical model chunks text into more meaningful units, such as words or semantic groups [S1].

record.text: Experiments show that fixed-width pooling, referred to as H-Net (pool), performs significantly worse than all other H-Net variants, validating that this approach is not effective [S3]. In comparison, the one-stage dynamic chunking model, H-Net (1-stage), is stronger than the heuristic-based H-Net (space) variant [S3]. The two-stage dynamic chunking model, H-Net (2-stage), is significantly better than the one-stage version, demonstrating that iterated dynamic chunking learns nested hierarchies [S3]. These dynamic methods scale better than static tokenizers, crossing over the tokenization-based Transformer baseline at 100B bytes for one-stage and 30B bytes for two-stage at the XL scale [S3]. The advantage of learnable dynamic chunking widens progressively with additional training data [S3]. Fixed-width pooling is categorized as a static hierarchical mechanism in related work tables, distinct from H-Net's dynamic approach [S1].
